learningObjectives.title: Causes of crime and attitudes to lawbreakers
The aims of punishment (deterrence, retribution, reformation)

questions.q: Which set correctly names the three aims of punishment on the AQA specification?
questions.explain: The specification identifies deterrence, retribution and reformation as the three aims of punishment.

questions.q: What does 'retribution' as an aim of punishment mean?
options: Making the offender pay for what they have done
Putting others off committing the same crime
Changing the offender so they do not reoffend
Keeping the public safe from the offender
questions.explain: Retribution is the idea that criminals should get their 'just deserts' and pay for the wrong they have done.

questions.q: What does 'deterrence' as an aim of punishment mean?
options: Putting people off committing crime through fear of punishment
Helping the offender become a better person
Taking revenge on behalf of the victim
Removing a dangerous person from society
questions.explain: Deterrence aims to discourage the offender and others from committing crime by making them fear the consequences.

questions.q: What does 'reformation' as an aim of punishment mean?
options: Changing an offender's behaviour so they do not offend again
Making an example of the offender to warn others
Ensuring the punishment matches the seriousness of the crime
Compensating the victim for their loss
questions.explain: Reformation aims to change the offender's attitudes and behaviour so they can rejoin society as a law-abiding person.

questions.q: Which of the following is commonly given as a cause of crime in this theme?
questions.explain: Causes of crime studied in this theme include poverty, upbringing, mental illness, addiction, greed and hate.

questions.q: In Matthew's Gospel, when Peter asked how often he should forgive, Jesus replied not seven times but...
questions.explain: Jesus told Peter to forgive 'seventy times seven', teaching that forgiveness should have no limit.

questions.q: The teaching 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' is found in which part of the Bible?
questions.explain: This teaching about proportionate retribution comes from the Old Testament (Exodus).

questions.q: What is the term for the belief that life is holy and given by God?
questions.explain: Sanctity of life is the belief that life is sacred and belongs to God, often used against the death penalty.

questions.q: Which aim of punishment is best reflected by the teaching 'an eye for an eye'?
questions.explain: 'An eye for an eye' suggests a proportionate payback for wrongdoing, which is the aim of retribution.

questions.q: What did Jesus mean when he taught his followers to 'turn the other cheek'?
options: They should respond to wrongdoing without seeking revenge
They should always report criminals to the authorities
They should ignore all laws they disagree with
They should demand equal punishment for offenders
questions.explain: 'Turn the other cheek' teaches non-retaliation and responding to harm peacefully rather than with revenge.

questions.q: Which argument do many religious believers use AGAINST the death penalty?
options: Only God has the right to take a life
Revenge is the main purpose of punishment
It is the cheapest form of punishment
questions.explain: The sanctity of life argument holds that because life is God-given, humans should not take it through capital punishment.

questions.q: Reformation as an aim of punishment fits best with which Christian belief?
options: People can change and be forgiven
God does not care about criminals
Justice means matching harm with harm
questions.explain: Reformation reflects the Christian belief in repentance, forgiveness and the possibility that anyone can change.

questions.q: Why do some Christians support the death penalty?
options: The Old Testament permits capital punishment for some crimes
Jesus commanded his followers to execute criminals
It guarantees offenders will be reformed
The New Testament states it must always be used
questions.explain: Some Christians point to Old Testament laws that allow the death penalty for serious offences to justify their support.

questions.q: Why might a Christian avoid harshly condemning someone who steals food because of poverty?
options: Christians teach compassion and consider the causes of crime
Christians believe stealing is never wrong
Christians reject all forms of punishment
Christians think the poor cannot sin
questions.explain: Christian teaching on compassion encourages understanding the circumstances, such as poverty, that lead people to crime.

questions.q: Christian teaching that believers should forgive others is mainly based on the belief that...
options: God forgives human sin, so people should forgive one another
Forgiveness always removes the need for punishment
Only priests have the power to forgive
Forgiveness is required by the state
questions.explain: Because Christians believe God forgives their sins, they are called to show the same forgiveness to others.

questions.q: A prison introduces education classes and job training to help inmates lead honest lives after release. Which aim of punishment is this?
questions.explain: Providing skills and education to change future behaviour is an example of reformation.

questions.q: A government introduces very harsh, well-publicised sentences hoping people will be too frightened to break the law. Which aim of punishment is this?
questions.explain: Using fear of punishment to put people off crime is the aim of deterrence.

questions.q: A murder victim's family publicly state they hold no hatred and wish the offender no harm. Which Christian value are they most clearly showing?
questions.explain: Choosing not to seek revenge and letting go of hatred is an example of Christian forgiveness.

questions.q: A Christian argues that a person who steals to feed an addiction needs treatment and support rather than only punishment. Which idea best supports this view?
options: Understanding the causes of crime can guide a compassionate response
Retribution is the only valid aim of punishment
Addiction is not a recognised cause of crime
All lawbreakers deserve the death penalty
questions.explain: Recognising causes such as addiction can lead believers to favour help and reformation alongside justice.

questions.q: Which of the following is described in this theme as a possible cause of crime?
questions.explain: Hate, alongside poverty, upbringing, mental illness, addiction and greed, is listed as a cause of crime.

specSource: AQA GCSE Religious Studies A specification; Theme E: Religion, Crime & Punishment
